name: Spironolactone
summary: The prototype mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, with a 30% mortality reduction in HFrEF (RALES); also a cornerstone of resistant-hypertension, cirrhosis-ascites, and primary hyperaldosteronism therapy.
mechanism: Competitive aldosterone receptor antagonism in the distal nephron promotes sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium and hydrogen; the active metabolite is canrenone.

dosing.adult: Heart failure: 25 mg once daily (12.5 mg if at risk of hyperkalemia), max 50 mg/day; hypertension: 25–50 mg once daily (up to 100 mg/day divided)
dosing.renalAdjustment: Avoid in significant renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min)

safety.pregnancy: Not recommended — antiandrogenic effects on the male fetus
safety.lactation: Active metabolite canrenone excreted in breast milk
warnings: Hyperkalemia — highest risk with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium supplements, and NSAIDs
Gynecomastia and breast tenderness are dose-related
safety.overdose: Hyperkalemia and arrhythmias; treat with insulin/glucose, potassium binders, and dialysis if severe.

indications: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Ascites and edema in cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome
clinicalPearls: RALES made low-dose spironolactone standard in HFrEF — a 30% relative mortality reduction.
Gynecomastia is dose-related and the most common reason patients switch to eplerenone.
good: HFrEF, resistant hypertension, and cirrhosis ascites at low doses.
bad: Hyperkalemia, significant renal impairment, or gynecomastia-prone patients.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard pharmacology references (Goodman & Gilman, Katzung, Lexicomp-level standard facts). Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
